claims.text: A graph neural network with transfer learning can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will outperform current predictive models by at least 15% in mean absolute error.
The input materials may be high-entropy alloys in either an as-cast or annealed state.
The model will be trained using high-entropy-alloy compositions and corresponding thermal-conductivity values.
Transfer learning will leverage knowledge from similar material systems.
The training dataset will contain at least 100 high-entropy alloys with varied compositions and microstructures.
Laser flash is a standardized technique suitable for obtaining the thermal-conductivity values used by the model.
A graph neural network can learn complex relationships between material structure and thermal conductivity.
Lattice distortions affect phonon scattering and thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Grain boundaries affect phonon scattering and thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The model can capture the effects of lattice distortions, grain boundaries, and other microstructural features on phonon scattering and thermal conductivity.
The proposed model will achieve a thermal-conductivity mean absolute error below 0.5 W/m-K.
Current predictive models have a thermal-conductivity mean absolute error of 0.7 W/m-K.
The Debye-Callaway model is a current predictive baseline for the thermal conductivity of high-entropy alloys.
The approach is applicable to alloys containing three to five principal elements.
The approach is applicable over a temperature range of 300 K to 1000 K.
Model accuracy may depend on training-data quality and diversity, hyperparameter selection, and transfer-learning strategy.
The benchmark will be a blinded comparison of predictions and measurements for 20 high-entropy alloys with varied compositions and microstructures.
Low phonon thermal conductivity is operationally defined as less than 1.5 W/m-K.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction error exceeds 0.7 W/m-K or fewer than 80% of low-conductivity alloys are correctly identified.
